items.followUp: Use the kinetic molecular model to explain why a gas can be compressed more easily than a liquid.

rubric.why: Shows the basic idea that matter consists of particles that are in motion.
rubric.description: States that matter is made of particles in motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning particles and their motion.

rubric.why: Identifies the close arrangement and restricted motion of particles in a solid.
rubric.description: Describes solid particles as closely packed and vibrating about fixed positions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the solid-state description.

rubric.why: Distinguishes liquid particles from solid particles by their movement or forces.
rubric.description: Describes liquid particles as able to move or slide past one another, with weaker forces than in solids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the liquid-state description.

rubric.why: Identifies the large separation and freedom of movement of gas particles.
rubric.description: Describes gas particles as far apart, moving freely or randomly, with very weak forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the gas-state description.

modelAnswer: Matter consists of tiny particles that are in continuous motion and exert forces on one another.
In a solid, particles are closely packed; strong forces hold them in fixed positions, where they vibrate.
In a liquid, particles are less closely packed and can move or slide past one another because the forces are weaker.
In a gas, particles are far apart, move freely and randomly, and have very weak forces between them.
These differences in particle arrangement, motion and forces explain the different properties of the states of matter.

items.followUp: Define a physical quantity and state its two parts.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of measurement as comparison with a standard.
rubric.description: Defines measurement as comparing a quantity with a standard unit.

rubric.why: Checks both components of a measured quantity.
rubric.description: Names the numerical value and the unit as the two parts of a measurement.

modelAnswer: Measurement is the comparison of a physical quantity with a standard unit of the same kind.
The two parts of a measurement are its numerical value and its unit.

items.followUp: Name three SI base quantities and three quantities derived from them.

rubric.why: Checks examples of independent base quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any three correct base quantities.

rubric.why: Checks examples of quantities formed from base quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any three correct derived quantities.

modelAnswer: Three base quantities are length, mass and time.
Three derived quantities are area, volume and speed.

items.followUp: Why is it important to use the same standard unit when comparing measurements made by different people?

rubric.why: Checks that a standard unit provides a common basis for comparison.
rubric.description: Explains that a standard unit allows quantities to be compared uniformly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the common comparison basis.

rubric.why: Checks the value of standard units for reliable results or communication.
rubric.description: Explains that standard units give consistent, understandable results and avoid confusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid consequence of using standard units.

modelAnswer: A standard unit provides a common basis for comparing measurements.
It gives consistent results and avoids confusion when measurements are recorded or communicated.

items.followUp: What does the slope of a distance-time graph represent, and what does the area under a speed-time graph represent?

rubric.why: Checks the axes or quantities represented in a distance-time graph.
rubric.description: Defines a distance-time graph as distance plotted against time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct graph description.

rubric.why: Checks the axes or quantities represented in a speed-time graph.
rubric.description: Defines a speed-time graph as speed plotted against time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct graph description.

modelAnswer: A distance-time graph shows how distance changes with time, with distance plotted against time.
A speed-time graph shows how speed changes with time, with speed plotted against time.

items.followUp: State two effects a force can have on the motion of an object.

rubric.why: Checks that force can change an object's state of motion or speed.
rubric.description: States that a force can start or stop motion, or change an object's speed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct change in state of motion or speed.

rubric.why: Checks another possible effect of a force.
rubric.description: States that a force can change an object's direction or shape.

modelAnswer: A force may start or stop an object, or change its speed.
A force may also change the direction of motion or the shape of an object.

items.followUp: A 2 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s². Find the force acting on it and state its SI unit.

rubric.why: Checks the statement of Newton's second law or its equation for constant mass.
rubric.description: States that force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum, or gives F = ma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the law or its equation.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of the newton in terms of mass and acceleration.
rubric.description: Defines one newton as the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct unit definition.

modelAnswer: Newton’s second law states that the force acting on a body is directly proportional to the rate of change of its momentum and acts in the same direction.
For constant mass, F = ma.
The SI unit of force is the newton (N).
One newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².

items.followUp: Explain what happens to a boat when a person jumps from it onto the river bank, using Newton's third law.

rubric.why: Checks that the jumper exerts a backward force on the boat while jumping.
rubric.description: States that the jumper pushes the boat backward, forming an action-reaction interaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the push or action-reaction pair.

rubric.why: Checks the resulting backward motion of the boat and its effect on the jump.
rubric.description: Explains that the boat moves away from the bank, so the jumper may fail to reach it and fall into the water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the boat's recoil and its consequence for the jumper.

modelAnswer: As the person jumps, they push the boat backward with their feet.
The boat recoils away from the river bank; the increasing separation can cause the jumper to miss the bank and fall into the water.
